unit.title: Reading Well
unit.summary: Six lessons on how to read the Bible well: naming the presuppositions we bring, reading each kind of writing as it was meant (figures of speech, poetry, irony and symbol), hearing a passage in its culture, date, audience and language, telling description from command, letting Scripture interpret Scripture instead of building on one verse, and holding the Bible's paradoxes together.

lessons.title: There Is No Plain Reading: Presuppositions, Exegesis and Eisegesis
lessons.question: Can't I just read the Bible plainly? Why do sincere people read the same verse and reach opposite conclusions?
lessons.bigIdea: Everyone reads through glasses. We cannot remove our presuppositions, but we can name them, test them and let the text correct them. Good reading draws meaning out of the text (exegesis) instead of pouring our own ideas into it (eisegesis), and it checks every conclusion against the character of God revealed in Jesus.

sections.heading: Everyone wears glasses
sections.body:
When people say "I just read the Bible plainly," they usually mean "I read it the way that seems obvious to me and my church." But what seems obvious depends on what we already believe: about God, about the Bible, about human beings, about how language works, and about what our tradition has taught us. These prior beliefs are called presuppositions. A presupposition is something you assume before you start reading, often without noticing it.

The Bible itself shows that reading is not automatic. When Ezra read the Law to the returned exiles, the Levites "gave the sense" so the people could understand (Neh 8:8). The Ethiopian official asked Philip, "How can I, except some man should guide me?" (Acts 8:30-31). Peter admits that some things in Paul's letters are "hard to be understood" and that people twist them (2 Pet 3:16). Even the disciples needed Jesus to open their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45).

This does not mean the Bible is unclear. The Reformers taught the clarity (perspicuity) of Scripture, but they meant that the central message of salvation is clear enough for ordinary people, not that every verse is plain. The Westminster Confession (1.7) says so directly: not all things in Scripture are equally plain, but what is needed for salvation is clearly set out. So the honest position is this: the heart of the message is clear, and the details need careful, humble reading.

sections.heading: Prolegomena: examining the glasses
sections.body:
Theologians have a name for the study of these starting assumptions: prolegomena. The word is Greek and means "things said beforehand." In a book of theology, the prolegomena is the opening part that asks the first questions before any doctrine is taught. What is revelation? How can humans know God at all? What kind of book is the Bible? How should it be read, and who has authority to interpret it? Large works of theology, such as Herman Bavinck's *Reformed Dogmatics*, give a whole volume to these questions.

You do not need to write a book of prolegomena, but you do have one. Five presuppositions shape almost every reading. (1) God: what is God like? (2) Scripture: is it a rule book, a law code, a story, a witness, or all of these? (3) Humans: can we understand God, or does our fallen nature bend what we hear (1 Cor 2:14)? (4) History: can miracles happen, and does the text describe real events? (5) Purpose: why am I reading — to win an argument, to obey, to meet God?

The goal is not to have no presuppositions. That is impossible. The goal is to hold them in the open, where Scripture can confirm, challenge or correct them. Hebrews says we must come believing that God is and that he rewards those who seek him (Heb 11:6). That is a presupposition too, and the Bible asks for it.

sections.heading: Exegesis and eisegesis
sections.body:
Exegesis comes from Greek *ex* (out) and *hēgeomai* (to lead). It means leading the meaning out of the text: asking what the author was saying to his first hearers, in his language, genre and setting. Eisegesis comes from *eis* (into). It means reading our own ideas into the text and then finding them there. The learner's notes put it honestly: we mostly read into the text with preconceived ideas.

The same Greek root appears in a striking place. John says no one has ever seen God, but the only Son "has declared him" (John 1:18). The verb is *exēgēsato* — Jesus is the one who leads God out into view. Many Christians draw from this a principle for reading: Jesus is the Father's own exegesis, so he is the surest guide to what God is like.

No human reader does pure exegesis. In 1957 the scholar Rudolf Bultmann wrote an essay asking whether exegesis without presuppositions is possible, and his answer was no. But he also said that our first understanding must stay open to correction. Evangelical scholars such as Grant Osborne describe this as a spiral: we bring our questions to the text, the text answers and corrects us, and we come back with better questions. Signs that you have slipped into eisegesis: you lifted a verse out of its paragraph; your meaning is one the first hearers could not have understood; you decided the conclusion before you read; or the text happens to say exactly what you wanted.

sections.heading: "Because it is written": when a verse is used against God
sections.body:
The learner's notes point to a real danger: religion often proves a point simply because a verse says something, without asking whether that reading fits the nature of God. The Gospels show this clearly. In the wilderness, Satan quotes Scripture accurately (Ps 91:11-12) to tempt Jesus to test God. Jesus does not reply "that is not in the Bible." He replies, "It is written again" (Matt 4:6-7). One verse used against the whole witness of Scripture becomes a weapon.

Jesus also told the most careful Bible readers of his day that they searched the Scriptures, thinking they had life in them, yet refused to come to the very person the Scriptures were about (John 5:39-40). He said their tradition could "make the word of God of none effect" (Mark 7:9-13), and when they used the Sabbath law to condemn hungry disciples he quoted Hosea: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matt 12:7). The problem was not too much Bible but a reading cut off from God's heart.

Church history repeats the pattern. Verses were used to defend slavery, for example the "curse of Ham" — although Genesis 9:25 actually curses Canaan and says nothing about Africa or skin colour. Verses were used to justify crusades, persecution and abuse. Christians across traditions have answered with a test: Irenaeus used the "rule of faith" (the apostolic summary of the faith); Augustine taught that any reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood the text (Matt 22:37-40); Luther asked whether a reading "promotes Christ"; and many today ask, "Does this reading look like Jesus?" (Heb 1:3). The test has a risk too. If "the nature of God" means my own preferences, the test becomes another eisegesis. That is why God's character must itself be learned from the whole of Scripture, centred on Jesus — including his cross, his mercy and his warnings.

sections.heading: Why presuppositions matter so much
sections.body:
The learner's notes trace a chain: bad presuppositions and a poor view of human beings (anthropology) lead to bad Bible interpretation; bad interpretation leads to bad theology; bad theology to bad eschatology (beliefs about the end and God's future); bad eschatology to bad ecclesiology (beliefs about what the church is and does); and bad ecclesiology to an unhealthy way of life. The chain also runs the other way: healthy foundations bear healthy fruit.

You can test the chain with an example. If I assume God is mainly an angry judge who must be kept calm, I will read wrath texts first and mercy texts as exceptions. My theology will centre on avoiding punishment, my picture of the future will be mostly fear, my church will police behaviour, and my daily life may be anxious and harsh. If I assume, with John, that God is love (1 John 4:8) and that Jesus shows the Father (John 14:9), the same Bible will be read in a very different key — though I still have to take its warnings seriously.

Lesson 23 returns to this chain in detail. For now the point is simple: the most important work in Bible study happens before you open the page. Ask God to show you your glasses.

visuals.title: From presuppositions to lifestyle
visuals.intro: The learner's chain, read from root to fruit. Tap each link to see how a hidden assumption travels all the way into daily life.

links.label: Presuppositions and anthropology
links.detail: What I assume about God, Scripture and human beings before I read. Example: "God is mainly angry" or "God is like Jesus"; "humans are worthless" or "humans are image-bearers who fell."

links.label: Biblical interpretation
links.detail: My assumptions decide which verses feel central and which feel like exceptions, and how I read figures, stories and commands.

links.label: Theology
links.detail: From many readings I build a picture of who God is and what salvation means.

links.label: Eschatology
links.detail: That picture shapes what I expect God to do in the future: rescue, renewal, judgement, escape or restoration.

links.label: Ecclesiology
links.detail: What I expect for the future shapes what I think the church is for: a lifeboat, a family, a court, an outpost of the kingdom.

links.label: Lifestyle
links.detail: How the church is shaped becomes how people pray, treat outsiders, handle money and power, and live day by day.

visuals.title: Exegesis or eisegesis?
visuals.intro: Each card is a way someone has read a verse. Is it drawing meaning out of the text, or reading an idea into it?

items.text: "I can do all things through Christ" means I will win the championship if I believe hard enough.
items.why: Paul, writing in prison (Phil 1:13), is talking about contentment whether he is well fed or hungry (Phil 4:11-12). The strength is to endure any circumstance, not a promise of victory.

items.text: Christ gives Paul strength to be content in plenty and in hunger, so believers can trust him in every situation.
items.why: This follows the flow of the paragraph and the situation of the writer.

items.text: "I know the thoughts that I think toward you" is God's personal promise that my career plan will succeed this year.
items.why: The promise was given to a whole people in exile in Babylon, and it would be fulfilled after seventy years (Jer 29:10). It shows God's faithful purposes, but it is not a guarantee of a personal plan.

items.text: "Where two or three are gathered" assures the community that Jesus stands behind its careful decisions about a brother who sins.
items.why: The saying comes at the end of instructions about church discipline with two or three witnesses (Matt 18:16). It is about Jesus' presence in the community's judgement, not mainly about small prayer meetings.

items.text: "Touch not mine anointed" means no one may question or correct a pastor.
items.why: In context God protects the patriarchs from foreign kings. Prophets and leaders in Scripture were regularly tested, and the Bereans were praised for checking Paul (Acts 17:11).

items.text: "Ye are the temple of God" is a warning to a divided church that together they are God's dwelling place.
items.why: The "ye" is plural in Greek and the chapter is about division (1 Cor 3:3-4). Paul applies the temple image to the individual body later, in 1 Cor 6:19.

items.text: "Prove me now herewith" guarantees wealth to anyone who gives to this ministry.
items.why: Malachi addresses covenant Israel bringing tithes to the temple storehouse to support Levites and the poor. God's generosity is real, but turning this into a fixed financial formula ignores its setting.

items.text: "Train up a child" is read as a wise general pattern, not an iron guarantee, because it is a proverb.
items.why: Proverbs speak in general truths. Some proverbs even sit side by side and seem to contradict each other (Prov 26:4-5), which shows they are wisdom for situations, not mechanical promises.

items.text: "Behold, I stand at the door" is Jesus calling a lukewarm church in Laodicea back to fellowship with him.
items.why: The words are spoken to a church. Using them as an invitation to individuals can be a fair secondary application, but the first meaning is about a congregation.

items.text: The curse in Genesis 9 shows that God approved the enslavement of Africans.
items.why: Noah's words are about Canaan, not Ham, and say nothing about Africa or skin colour. The reading was created by slave-holding societies looking for a proof-text.

items.text: "Hate his father and mother" means a disciple must cut off his family.
items.why: In Hebrew idiom "hate" can mean "love less" (Gen 29:30-31). Matthew gives the same saying as loving family more than Jesus (Matt 10:37). It is about first loyalty, not abandonment.

visuals.title: Five honest questions before I conclude
visuals.intro: A short habit for catching yourself reading in.

steps.label: What do I already believe?
steps.detail: Write down what you expect the passage to say before you read it. Now you can see your glasses.

steps.label: What did it mean then?
steps.detail: Ask who wrote it, to whom, and why. What could the first hearers have understood?

steps.label: What does the context say?
steps.detail: Read the whole paragraph and chapter. Does the surrounding text support my reading?

steps.label: Does it look like Jesus?
steps.detail: Does my conclusion fit the character of God shown in Jesus and in the whole story of Scripture?

steps.label: Who reads it differently?
steps.detail: Find a careful reader from another tradition. Why do they see it differently? What might I be missing?

voices.text: Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures, or any part of them, but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbour, does not yet understand them as he ought.
voices.source: On Christian Doctrine 1.36.40 (trans. J. F. Shaw)

voices.text: If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect.

views.name: Author-centred grammatical-historical reading
views.who: Most evangelical seminaries; Walter Kaiser, Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, Klein, Blomberg and Hubbard; E. D. Hirsch in literary theory; the Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (1982)
views.summary: The meaning of a text is what its author intended to communicate to his first readers, discovered through grammar, history and genre. Presuppositions are real, but careful method can correct them, and the text can say no to us.
views.strengths: It gives the text its own voice and protects against making the Bible say anything we like. It gives churches shared rules for testing readings.
views.critiques: We never have perfect access to an author's mind. It can treat the Bible like any ancient document and underplay the Spirit and the Christ-centred reading the New Testament writers themselves practised (Luke 24:27).

views.name: Hermeneutical spiral / two horizons
views.who: Hans-Georg Gadamer (philosophy); Anthony Thiselton, Grant Osborne, Kevin Vanhoozer (Christian scholars)
views.summary: Understanding is a conversation between the horizon of the text and the horizon of the reader. Our pre-understanding is a starting point, not a final verdict; each return to the text refines it.
views.strengths: Honest about how reading actually works. It explains why mature readers keep finding new things without abandoning old truths.
views.critiques: Without firm anchors it can slide into treating every reading as provisional. Critics ask how we know when the spiral has reached a reliable meaning.

views.name: Reader-response / interpretive communities
views.who: Stanley Fish and other literary theorists; some liberation and contextual readers
views.summary: Meaning arises when readers and communities engage the text. What a passage means depends partly on who is reading and why.
views.strengths: It exposes how power and culture shape readings and gives a voice to readers whose experience was ignored, such as the poor or the colonised.
views.critiques: If meaning lives mainly in the reader, the text can no longer correct the reader, and eisegesis becomes a method. Most Christian traditions reject the strong form.

views.name: Reading within the Church's rule of faith
views.who: Catholic (*Dei Verbum* 12), Eastern Orthodox (the Fathers and tradition), and classical Protestants who use the creeds; Irenaeus, Augustine
views.summary: Scripture should be read in the same Spirit in which it was written, within the faith handed down by the apostles and summarised in the rule of faith and the creeds. The community guards against private readings.
views.strengths: It protects against individual novelty and keeps readers in conversation with two thousand years of saints.
views.critiques: Tradition can itself become the unexamined presupposition Jesus warned about (Mark 7:13). Protestants worry the church's reading can override the text.

views.name: Jesus as the decisive lens
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson ("Jesus is perfect theology"), Tommy Miller; in older forms Luther ("what promotes Christ") and many Church Fathers
views.summary: The most important presupposition is a person. Jesus is the Father's own exegesis (John 1:18) and the exact imprint of his nature (Heb 1:3), so every reading must be tested by whether it reveals a God who looks like Jesus. A proof-text that produces an un-Christlike God has been misread.
views.strengths: It answers "because it is written" with Jesus' own method (Matt 12:7, John 5:39-40). It has historically protected against using verses to justify violence and abuse.
views.critiques: Who decides what is "Christlike"? Critics such as D. A. Carson and Paul Copan warn it can become a filter for modern preferences, drift toward Marcion's split between the Testaments, and overlook that Jesus affirmed the Old Testament (Matt 5:17-18) and spoke of judgement (Matt 25:46). Defenders reply that the lens includes the cross, Jesus' warnings and his love, and aims to read every text, not to delete any.

misreadings.topic: "I don't interpret the Bible, I just read what it says"
misreadings.popular: Many sincere believers feel that interpretation means twisting Scripture. They want to submit to the Bible, not to scholars, so they say they simply read it and do what it says.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible itself shows interpretation happening: the Levites explaining the Law (Neh 8:8), Jesus opening the Scriptures (Luke 24:27), Philip guiding the Ethiopian (Acts 8:31), Peter warning that Paul is hard to understand (2 Pet 3:16). Everyone interprets; the question is whether we do it carefully and humbly.
misreadings.defence: Careful evangelical scholars agree that everyone interprets, but they rightly defend the clarity of Scripture: the core gospel is plain enough for any honest reader (Westminster Confession 1.7). The desire to submit to the text is healthy; it simply needs to include submitting to its genre and context.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Readers who think they do not interpret cannot see their own presuppositions, so they often confuse their tradition with the Bible and treat anyone who disagrees as rejecting God's word.

misreadings.topic: "If everyone has presuppositions, every reading is equally valid"
misreadings.popular: Some people hear that there is no plain reading and conclude that all interpretations are just opinions, so no one can say a reading is wrong.
misreadings.inContext: Admitting we wear glasses does not mean there is nothing to see. Texts have words, grammar, settings and purposes that rule out many readings. The Bereans checked Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11), assuming some readings fit better than others.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox scholars all insist the text has a real meaning that can correct us. Even Gadamer held that the text makes a claim on the reader. Humility about our readings is a virtue; giving up on truth is not.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Without this balance, readers swing between arrogance ("my reading is plain") and despair ("no one can know"). Healthy reading holds convictions with humility.

discuss: Which verse have you heard used in two opposite ways? What presuppositions might explain the difference?
Name one presupposition you brought to the Bible from your family, church or culture. Has Scripture ever challenged it?
Satan quoted Scripture correctly in Matthew 4:6. What does that teach us about proof-texting?
Is "Does this reading look like Jesus?" a safe test? How do we stop it becoming "Does this reading look like me?"
Where has the church used "because it is written" to justify harm? How should we respond today?
practice: Before reading a passage this week, write down what you expect it to say. Afterward, note where the text surprised you.
Take a favourite verse and read the whole chapter around it. Does the verse still mean what you thought?
Ask someone from a different church tradition how they read a passage you care about, and listen without arguing.

lessons.title: Literalism or Literature? How the Bible Speaks
lessons.question: What is the problem with reading the Bible literally? Does God really ride on a cherub and fly on the wings of the wind?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible is literature: God speaks through poems, stories, laws, letters, proverbs and visions, full of metaphor, irony and imagery. To take it seriously is to read each part the way it was meant to be read — literally where it means to be literal, figuratively where it speaks in figures.

sections.heading: Two meanings of "literal"
sections.body:
The word "literal" is used in two very different ways. In the older Christian tradition, the "literal sense" meant the meaning the author intended to communicate, including his figures of speech. Thomas Aquinas taught that when Scripture speaks of God's "arm", the literal sense is not a body part but God's power. The Reformers, who championed the literal sense, meant the same thing: the natural meaning of the words in their kind of writing.

In popular speech today, "literal" often means something else: taking every word at face value, whatever kind of writing it is. This is better called literalism. Nobody is fully consistent in it. No one believes God is a rock made of stone (Ps 18:2), or that Jesus is a wooden door (John 10:9), or that trees have hands to clap (Isa 55:12).

Literalism can do real harm. Jesus said that if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out (Matt 5:29-30). He was using hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration — to show how seriously to treat sin. The church historian Eusebius reports that the young Origen took Matthew 19:12 literally and castrated himself, an act Eusebius describes as zeal without mature judgement (historians debate the report). Even the strongest statements of biblical inerrancy, such as the Chicago Statement of 1978, say that hyperbole, round numbers and everyday descriptions of nature do not count as errors. Reading as literature is not a lower view of the Bible; it is reading it as God gave it.

sections.heading: Test case: Psalm 18:9-10
sections.body:
"He bowed the heavens also, and came down: and darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind" (Ps 18:9-10). The same song appears in 2 Samuel 22, where it is David's song after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. Around these lines the earth shakes, smoke comes from God's nostrils, fire from his mouth, and he shoots lightning like arrows (Ps 18:7-8; Ps 18:14).

The historical accounts of David's escapes record no earthquake or storm. At one point Saul simply has to turn back because the Philistines have invaded (1 Sam 23:26-28). So the psalm is not a weather report. It is a poet painting the inner meaning of his rescue with the biggest images he has: when I cried, the God of heaven and earth moved for me (Ps 18:6; Ps 18:16-19).

The images also had a background. In the Canaanite texts found at Ugarit (from about the 13th century BC), the storm god Baal is called "rider of the clouds." Israel's poets took this kind of language and gave it to the LORD (Ps 68:4; Ps 104:3; Deut 33:26; Isa 19:1). The message to the first hearers was pointed: it is not Baal but the LORD who rules the storm. The cherub is the winged guardian of God's throne, pictured over the ark (Exod 25:18-22; 1 Sam 4:4) and in Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot (Ezek 10:1-22). Later, Jesus applied the cloud-rider image from Daniel 7:13 to himself before the high priest (Mark 14:62), and his disciples, watching wind and sea obey him, asked, "What manner of man is this?" (Mark 4:41).

sections.heading: Genres: each kind of writing has its own rules
sections.body:
A genre is a kind of writing. We already know how genres work: we do not read a newspaper report, a love song and a cartoon in the same way. The Bible contains many genres. Narrative tells what happened, often without commenting on whether it was good (Judg 21:25). Law gives Israel's covenant instructions. Poetry, like the Psalms, speaks in images and emotion. Wisdom, like Proverbs, gives general truths for living. Prophecy calls God's people back to covenant faithfulness and speaks of what God will do. Gospels tell the life of Jesus as good news. Letters address particular churches and their problems. Apocalyptic, like Daniel and Revelation, uses dramatic symbols to unveil God's view of history.

Mistakes in genre lead to mistakes in meaning. A proverb read as a promise becomes a broken promise (Prov 22:6). A psalm of anger read as a command becomes a call to cruelty (Ps 137:9). A vision read as a newspaper becomes a timetable of news events. The deep study on hermeneutics walks through each genre in detail.

sections.heading: Pictures and comparisons: figures of speech
sections.body:
A figure of speech says something in a non-literal way to make it more vivid or true to experience. The main ones in the Bible are these.

Analogy: explaining something by comparing it to something familiar ("as a father pitieth his children", Ps 103:13). Simile: an open comparison using "like" or "as" ("like a tree planted by the rivers", Ps 1:3). Metaphor: saying one thing is another ("The LORD is my shepherd", Ps 23:1; "Go ye, and tell that fox", Luke 13:32). Parable: a short story from everyday life that carries a surprise about God's kingdom (Luke 15:3-7). Imagery: a cluster of pictures that paint a scene, as in Psalm 18. Anthropomorphism: describing God with human features or feelings — his hand, eyes, smelling a sacrifice (Gen 8:21; Isa 59:1). The Bible itself warns that God "is not a man" (Num 23:19), so these are true pictures, not physical descriptions.

Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration to make a point ("a camel to go through the eye of a needle", Mark 10:25). Merism: naming two opposites to mean everything between them ("the heaven and the earth" = all that exists, Gen 1:1; "my downsitting and mine uprising" = all I do, Ps 139:2). Idiom: a phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words ("gird up the loins of your mind" = get ready for action, 1 Pet 1:13). Apocalyptic symbol: an image that stands for a reality, often explained in the text itself — the stars are angels and the lampstands are churches (Rev 1:20), the beasts are kings (Dan 7:17), and the Lion of Judah turns out to be a slain Lamb (Rev 5:5-6).

sections.heading: The shape of the text: parallelism, chiasm and inclusio
sections.body:
Hebrew poetry does not rhyme sounds; it rhymes ideas. This is called parallelism: two or more lines that echo each other. In 1753 Robert Lowth described three types. Synonymous: the second line repeats the first in new words ("The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork", Ps 19:1). Antithetic: the second line gives the opposite ("A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother", Prov 10:1). Synthetic: the second line develops or completes the first, as in the growing steps of walking, standing and sitting with the wicked (Ps 1:1). Later scholars such as James Kugel and Robert Alter show that the second line usually sharpens the first: "A — and what is more, B." So read the lines together, not as separate facts.

A chiasm is a pattern where ideas are given in one order and then repeated in reverse (A-B-B-A), often with the main point at the centre. "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). In Hebrew, Genesis 9:6 runs "whoever sheds / the blood / of man // by man / his blood / shall be shed". Some scholars find chiasms across whole stories, such as the flood narrative, though they debate how many are intended.

An inclusio is a frame: a passage begins and ends with the same phrase to mark a unit and its theme. Psalm 8 opens and closes with "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Ps 8:1; Ps 8:9). The Beatitudes begin and end with "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt 5:3; Matt 5:10). Noticing the frame tells you what the whole passage is about.

sections.heading: Irony and sarcasm: Jesus was not always gentle in tone
sections.body:
Irony says one thing while meaning another, often the opposite. Sarcasm is irony with a sharp edge. If we miss the tone, we can take a line to mean its opposite. The learner's notes rightly say that Jesus used sarcasm to expose religious views that hid God's heart.

"Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel" (Matt 23:24) is hyperbole and sarcasm together: the religious leaders filter tiny insects from their drink but gulp down the largest unclean animal. "Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition" (Mark 7:9) uses the word *kalōs* ("well", "beautifully") ironically — most commentators hear it as "How skilfully you set aside God's command!" When warned that Herod wanted to kill him, Jesus said, "it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem" (Luke 13:33): the holy city, of all places, is the one that kills its prophets (Luke 13:34).

The Bible's other voices do the same. Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: perhaps your god is busy, or travelling, or asleep (1 Kgs 18:27). Paul tells the proud Corinthians, "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us" (1 Cor 4:8). Sarcasm in Scripture is never cruelty for its own sake; it exposes pride and religious pretence so that people can see clearly.

visuals.title: Psalm 18:9-10 through four lenses
visuals.intro: The same two verses read four ways. Which readings fit the kind of writing this is?
visuals.passage: He bowed the heavens also, and came down: and darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind. (KJV)

lenses.name: Wooden literal
lenses.who: A strict literalist approach (rarely held consistently by anyone)
lenses.reading: God physically lowered the sky, stood on darkness and flew through the air seated on a winged creature during David's rescue. The problem: the historical accounts of David's escapes describe no such event (1 Sam 23:26-28), and the same reading would make God breathe smoke (Ps 18:8). Even most readers who call themselves literal treat these lines as poetry.

lenses.name: Poetic and ancient Near Eastern
lenses.who: Most Old Testament scholars, e.g. Peter Craigie, Mark S. Smith, John Walton
lenses.reading: This is storm-god imagery, the language neighbouring peoples used of Baal, the "rider of the clouds." Israel's poets claimed it for the LORD (Ps 68:4; Ps 104:3). The poem says: the true ruler of heaven and storm came down to save me. It is true poetry, not false science.

lenses.name: Theological (throne and temple)
lenses.who: Jewish and Christian commentators; the Talmudic principle that "the Torah speaks in the language of human beings" as applied by Maimonides
lenses.reading: The cherub is the bearer of God's throne, above the ark in the Holy of Holies (1 Sam 4:4) and in Ezekiel's vision (Ezek 10:1-22). The God enthroned in his temple left his throne in answer to one man's cry (Ps 18:6). The picture teaches God's majesty and his nearness at once.

lenses.name: Christ-centred
lenses.who: Church Fathers and Christ-centred readers today (e.g. Augustine on the Psalms; Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd)
lenses.reading: The God who "bowed the heavens and came down" did so fully in the incarnation (John 1:14). Jesus claimed the cloud-rider role of Daniel 7:13 (Mark 14:62) and stilled the storm (Mark 4:41). Yet he came not with smoke and arrows but in humility and self-giving love, showing what the storm imagery was always pointing toward: a God who comes down to rescue.

visuals.title: Name that figure of speech
visuals.intro: Pick the figure each verse mainly uses. Some verses use more than one; the answer explains.

items.text: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."
items.why: God is said to be a shepherd without "like" or "as". The picture carries care, guidance and protection.

items.text: "He shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water."
items.why: An open comparison using "like": the righteous person is compared to a well-watered tree.

items.text: "Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel."
items.why: No one can swallow a camel. The exaggeration exposes misplaced priorities. It is also sarcastic, so "irony" is a fair second answer.

items.text: "Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition."
items.why: "Full well" (Greek *kalōs*) is praise used ironically: how skilfully you set God's word aside.

items.text: "Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising."
items.why: Two opposites (sitting and rising) stand for everything the psalmist does.

items.text: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."
items.why: "Heaven and earth" names the two ends to mean the whole universe.

items.text: "And the LORD smelled a sweet savour."
items.why: God is described with a human sense to show he received Noah's offering with pleasure.

items.text: "A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother."
items.why: Antithetic parallelism: the second line gives the opposite of the first.

items.text: "Gird up the loins of your mind."
items.why: Ancient people tucked up long robes to run or work. The idiom means "prepare your minds for action."

items.text: "If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out."
items.why: Jesus is not commanding self-harm. The exaggeration shows how seriously to deal with sin.

items.text: "Either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth."
items.why: Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: their god cannot hear because he is not real.

visuals.title: Literal sense or literalism?
visuals.intro: The literal sense is what the author meant. Literalism takes the words at face value regardless of genre.

rows.label: Ps 18:10 — rode upon a cherub
cells: God flew on a winged creature through the sky
The true Lord of the storm came down to rescue David

rows.label: Matt 5:29 — pluck out your eye
cells: Remove body parts that lead you into sin
Deal radically and urgently with sin

rows.label: John 10:9 — I am the door
cells: Jesus is a gate
Jesus is the way into God's safe flock and life

rows.label: Isa 55:12 — trees clap their hands
cells: Trees will grow hands
All creation will rejoice when God redeems his people

rows.label: Rev 7:1 — four corners of the earth
cells: The earth is a flat square
From every direction; the whole world

rows.label: Luke 14:26 — hate father and mother
cells: Disciples must despise their families
Love Jesus first, so much that other loves look small beside it

voices.text: The Torah speaks in the language of human beings.
voices.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 31b; applied to the Bible's bodily language about God by Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* 1.26

views.name: Literal-grammatical (the "normal sense")
views.who: Most evangelical scholars; the Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (1982); Walter Kaiser; dispensational scholars such as Charles Ryrie, who defined literal as normal usage including figures
views.summary: Read the Bible in its normal, plain sense, the way the author meant it, recognising figures of speech where the text signals them. History is history, poetry is poetry.
views.strengths: It anchors readers in the text and protects real history and miracles from being turned into mere symbols.
views.critiques: Who decides when a passage is figurative? Critics note the decision is often driven by prior theology, as in debates over the days of creation or the millennium.

views.name: Consistent literalism (popular form)
views.who: Much popular preaching; often summarised in David L. Cooper's "golden rule": when the plain sense makes common sense, seek no other sense
views.summary: Take the words at face value unless that is impossible. Figurative readings are suspected of explaining the Bible away.
views.strengths: It comes from reverence and a fear of liberal reinterpretation. It takes God's promises and the reality of events seriously.
views.critiques: "Common sense" is cultural: what looks plain to a modern reader may not be what an ancient poet meant. It struggles with poetry, apocalyptic and idiom, and no one applies it consistently (Ps 18:2).

views.name: Literary reading
views.who: Robert Alter, James Kugel, Leland Ryken, G. B. Caird, Meir Sternberg
views.summary: The Bible is great literature. Its meaning is carried by plot, character, repetition, wordplay, parallelism and structure, so readers must learn how ancient literature works.
views.strengths: It opens the artistry of the text and explains many puzzles that come from treating poems and stories as lists of propositions.
views.critiques: Some literary scholars set aside the question of historical truth. Evangelical scholars answer that artistry and history can coexist, as Luke shows (Luke 1:1-4).

views.name: The fourfold sense
views.who: John Cassian, Thomas Aquinas, medieval Catholic tradition; in related forms Orthodox reading and Hans Boersma
views.summary: Scripture has a literal sense (what happened or what was said) and, built on it, an allegorical sense (about Christ and the church), a moral sense (how to live) and an anagogical sense (our final hope). Aquinas insisted all other senses rest on the literal one.
views.strengths: It reads the whole Bible as pointing to Christ and feeds devotion and preaching.
views.critiques: In unskilled hands it allows almost any meaning. The Reformers and modern scholars pushed back toward the author's intended sense.

views.name: Accommodation and the Jesus lens
views.who: John Calvin (God "lisps" to us as a nurse to an infant, *Institutes* 1.13.1); Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Peter Enns, Eric Seibert
views.summary: God speaks in human language and within human ways of seeing. Bodily and storm imagery are accommodations, and some portraits of God reflect how ancient people perceived him. Jesus, the true image of God, shows which pictures are deepest.
views.strengths: It explains anthropomorphism and ancient imagery while keeping reverence for the text, and it has deep roots in Calvin and the Fathers.
views.critiques: Calvin's accommodation concerned the form of God's speech, not mistaken human views of God. Critics say the stronger modern version risks deciding which texts are "merely human" by our own standards. Defenders answer that the New Testament itself reads the Old in light of Christ (Heb 1:1-3).

misreadings.topic: Taking the Bible literally means taking it seriously
misreadings.popular: Many believers feel that if they treat any passage as figurative, they are weakening the Bible. Taking every word literally feels like the safest and most faithful choice.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible's authors chose poems, parables, hyperbole and visions on purpose. Reading a psalm as a psalm is obeying the author, not doubting him. Jesus rebuked his disciples for being too literal when he spoke of the "leaven of the Pharisees" (Matt 16:6-12).
misreadings.defence: Traditional evangelical scholars agree. The Chicago Statement on Inerrancy (1978, Article XIII) says hyperbole, round numbers and observational descriptions of nature are not errors. Their concern is that real history, such as the resurrection, not be turned into mere symbol (1 Cor 15:14). Both sides agree: read literally what is meant literally.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Literalism can make the Bible look foolish to outsiders, can produce harm (Matt 5:29), and can hide the beauty and force of God's chosen ways of speaking.

misreadings.topic: The "eye of the needle" was a small gate in Jerusalem
misreadings.popular: A common sermon explanation says there was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called "the Needle's Eye". A camel could squeeze through only by kneeling and removing its load, so the rich can enter the kingdom if they humble themselves.
misreadings.inContext: There is no ancient evidence for such a gate. Jesus used hyperbole to describe something impossible; the Babylonian Talmud uses a similar image of an elephant passing through a needle's eye (Berakhot 55b). The disciples understood him: "Who then can be saved?" Jesus answered, "With men it is impossible, but not with God" (Mark 10:26-27).
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as R. T. France and Craig Keener agree that the gate story is a later invention. The point is not that salvation is hard work for the rich, but that it is God's miracle for everyone.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The gate story turns grace into effort and softens Jesus' shocking image. Recognising hyperbole restores his real message.

discuss: Before this lesson, how would you have explained Psalm 18:9-10? What changed?
Why might Israel's poets have borrowed language used of Baal and applied it to the LORD?
Which figure of speech do you find hardest to spot? Why?
Does it surprise you that Jesus used sarcasm? How should that shape the way we read his words to the Pharisees?
How can we tell when a passage is meant to be read as history and when as poetry or symbol?
Is there a passage you were taught to read literally that may be a figure of speech, or the other way round?
practice: Read Psalm 18 aloud in one sitting. Mark every image of God and ask what each one says about him.
Read Matthew 23 and underline every line that uses hyperbole, irony or sarcasm. What is Jesus exposing?
Find one example of parallelism in Proverbs and one inclusio in the Psalms, and explain them to someone else.

lessons.title: Culture, Date, Audience and Language
lessons.question: If we read a message or an idiom without the culture of its time, could we understand something completely different? How much does context, dating, audience and language change the meaning?
lessons.bigIdea: The Bible was written for us but not to us. Every book was first spoken to real people in a real culture, time and language. When we learn who was speaking, to whom, when, why and in what words, the message does not become smaller; it becomes clear, and it can then speak to us with its true force.

sections.heading: Written for us, not to us
sections.body:
The Old Testament scholar John Walton often says that the Bible was written for us but not to us. The learner's notes say something similar: the Bible was not written to us but given to us. Every book had a first audience. Paul wrote to believers in Corinth, Rome and Philippi; the prophets spoke to Israel and Judah; Revelation was sent to seven named churches in Asia (Rev 1:4; Rev 1:11). We are reading someone else's letters, and the message reaches us through them.

This matters because writers leave out what their first readers already knew. When Paul writes "Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me" (1 Cor 7:1), we are hearing one side of a conversation. When he speaks of "the present distress" (1 Cor 7:26), the Corinthians knew what he meant; we have to work it out. Walton's advice is that we must join the first audience in our imagination — learn what they knew — before we can hear how the text applies to us.

This is not a way of escaping the Bible's authority. It is a way of submitting to it. If God chose to speak through real people in a real time, then taking that time seriously is part of taking God seriously (Heb 1:1).

sections.heading: Building the context: who, to whom, when, why
sections.body:
Context has several layers. The literary context is the paragraph, book and whole Bible around a verse. The historical context is the time, place and events. The cultural context is the shared customs and values. The language context is the words, idioms and grammar of Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek.

Dating can change the picture. Revelation is usually dated to about AD 95, near the end of the emperor Domitian's reign, following Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30.3); a minority of scholars date it to the late 60s under Nero. Either way it was written to churches facing pressure from Rome and its imperial cult, which shapes how we read its beasts and its call to endure (Rev 13:1-10; Rev 2:10). The book of Daniel is dated by traditional scholars to the 6th century BC and by most critical scholars to about 165 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV. Each dating leads readers to hear its visions differently (Dan 7:1-28). These are debated questions, and fair readers name them rather than hide them.

Purpose matters too. John tells us why he wrote: "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ" (John 20:31). Luke wrote so that Theophilus might know the certainty of what he had been taught (Luke 1:1-4). Knowing the purpose helps us see why a book includes some things and leaves out others.

sections.heading: Cultural keys: honour, patronage, covenant and the ancient picture of the world
sections.body:
Honour and shame. In the ancient Mediterranean world, a person's worth was largely their public reputation in the eyes of family and village. Jesus "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:2): crucifixion was meant to destroy honour, and the gospel turns that shame into glory. Many readers in South Asia, Africa and the Middle East feel this world immediately, because their own cultures are built around family honour.

Patronage and grace. Society ran on patrons (benefactors with resources) and clients (those who received favour and owed loyalty and praise in return). Jesus mentions rulers who are called "benefactors" (Luke 22:25), and a centurion is commended for building a synagogue (Luke 7:4-5). The Greek word for grace, *charis*, belonged to this world: a gift that creates a relationship and calls for a grateful response. Paul's "free gift" language (Rom 5:15) would have sounded like the generosity of the greatest patron of all.

Covenant. Israel's covenant with God echoes the treaty forms of the ancient Near East, where a great king recalls what he has done for a people and then sets out obligations, blessings and curses. Exodus 20 begins, "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt" (Exod 20:2): rescue comes first, then commands. Deuteronomy's blessings and curses (Deut 28:1-68) follow the same pattern. Scholars debate whether Hittite or Assyrian treaties are the closer model.

Ancient cosmology. Ancient peoples pictured a solid dome (the "firmament", Hebrew *raqia*) holding back waters above (Gen 1:6-8), the earth set on pillars (1 Sam 2:8), with four corners (Isa 11:12; Rev 7:1). God spoke within that picture of the world to teach who made it and why, not to give a lesson in modern science. Readers disagree on how far this applies to Genesis 1, but most agree God did not first correct ancient cosmology before speaking.

sections.heading: When an idiom loses its culture
sections.body:
An idiom is a phrase whose meaning comes from its culture, not from its individual words. Read without its culture, an idiom can mean something totally different — exactly the danger the learner's notes describe.

"If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother... he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26). In Hebrew idiom, "love" and "hate" can mean "choose first" and "choose second". Jacob "loved also Rachel more than Leah", and Leah is then called "hated" (Gen 29:30-31). Matthew reports the saying as "He that loveth father or mother more than me" (Matt 10:37). "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated" (Mal 1:2-3; Rom 9:13) is about choosing, not emotion. The "horn of my salvation" (Ps 18:2; Luke 1:69) means mighty strength, from the image of a strong animal's horns. When the KJV speaks of the "bowels of Jesus Christ" (Phil 1:8), it renders the Greek *splanchna*, the inner organs, which were seen as the seat of deep feeling; modern versions say "affection" or "compassion".

Some idioms are still debated. "Thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head" (Prov 25:21-22; Rom 12:20) has been read as burning shame that leads to repentance, as a link to an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried coals on the head (known from a late Demotic text), or as simple generosity — giving live coals to a neighbour whose fire has gone out. All agree on the context: overcome evil with good (Rom 12:21).

sections.heading: Language texture that does not cross over
sections.body:
The learner's notes make a second point: some words and textures cannot carry their full essence into another language. This is true. Hebrew loves wordplay. God forms the human (*adam*) from the ground (*adamah*) (Gen 2:7). Amos sees a basket of summer fruit (*qayits*) and hears that the end (*qets*) has come (Amos 8:1-2). Jeremiah sees an almond branch (*shaqed*) and God says he is watching (*shoqed*) over his word (Jer 1:11-12). In English the connection disappears.

In John 3, Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born *anōthen*, a Greek word that can mean "again" or "from above". Nicodemus hears "again" and asks how a man can re-enter his mother's womb (John 3:3-4). Jesus means "from above", by the Spirit. A few verses later, the same word *pneuma* means both "wind" and "Spirit" (John 3:8). No single English word can hold both senses. Some words are so rich that no translation word fits: Hebrew *hesed* is rendered "mercy", "lovingkindness", "steadfast love" or "loyal love" (Ps 136:1), and Greek *pistis* can mean faith, trust or faithfulness.

This is why translators must interpret. Some translations stay close to the original words (formal equivalence, like the KJV, ESV or NASB); others aim to carry the meaning in natural language (functional or dynamic equivalence, like the NLT). Each choice gains something and loses something. The best habit is to compare several translations, learn a few key words, and use good study notes. Lesson 4 covers translation in depth.

visuals.title: Building the context of a passage
visuals.intro: Walk through these questions before deciding what a passage means for you.

steps.label: Who wrote it?
steps.detail: What do we know about the author, his situation and his relationship to the readers? Paul writing from prison sounds different from Paul planning a visit.

steps.label: To whom?
steps.detail: Who first heard it? Israel in exile, a mixed Jewish-Gentile church, a persecuted congregation? What did they already know?

steps.label: When?
steps.detail: What was happening in the world at the time? Which empire ruled? Is the date debated, and how would each date change the reading?

steps.label: Why?
steps.detail: What problem or purpose made the writer write? Look for statements of purpose.

steps.label: What kind of writing?
steps.detail: Story, law, poem, proverb, prophecy, letter, vision? Each genre has its own rules.

steps.label: What culture?
steps.detail: Which customs and values are assumed: honour and shame, patronage, kinship, covenant, the ancient picture of the world?

steps.label: Then: what does it say to us?
steps.detail: Having stood with the first hearers, ask what the same God is saying to us now, in light of Jesus.

visuals.title: Hearing the Prodigal Son: a modern reader and a first hearer
visuals.intro: Luke 15:11-32 as many modern readers hear it and as a first-century village audience may have heard it. Several cultural details come from Kenneth Bailey's work; some (such as whether asking for the inheritance meant wishing the father dead) are debated by scholars like Amy-Jill Levine.
columns: A first hearer would likely hear

rows.label: The audience (Luke 15:1-2)
cells: A story told to people who need to be saved
A story told because religious leaders complained that Jesus ate with sinners

rows.label: "Give me the portion of goods"
cells: A young man wanting independence
A shocking request that dishonours the father in front of the village

rows.label: The father runs (Luke 15:20)
cells: A happy, emotional welcome
An older man of honour running in public: he takes the shame on himself to reach his son first

rows.label: Robe, ring and shoes (Luke 15:22)

Full restoration of family status: the son is not a servant but a son

rows.label: The fatted calf (Luke 15:23)

A feast big enough for the whole village: public reconciliation

rows.label: The older brother (Luke 15:28-32)
cells: A side character
The real target: the father goes out to him too, and the story ends without telling us whether he comes in

visuals.title: John 3:3: born again or born from above?
visuals.intro: One Greek word with two senses, and how translations handle it.
visuals.original: ean mē tis gennēthē anōthen, ou dynatai idein tēn basileian tou theou

versions.name: KJV (1611)
versions.text: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
versions.note: Takes *anōthen* as "again", which matches Nicodemus' reply in John 3:4.

versions.name: NRSV (1989)
versions.text: No one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.
versions.note: Takes *anōthen* as "from above", matching John 3:31 where the same word means from above. A footnote gives "anew".

versions.name: NIV (2011)
versions.text: No one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again.
versions.note: Keeps "again" in the text and gives "from above" in a footnote, showing the translators knew both senses.

versions.name: Literal rendering
versions.text: Unless someone is born again / from above, he is not able to see the kingdom of God.
versions.note: Many scholars think John intends both senses: Nicodemus hears one, Jesus means the deeper one. No English word carries both.

voices.text: The Old Testament was written for us, but not to us.
voices.source: a principle Walton repeats across his work, e.g. *Wisdom for Faithful Reading* (2023); the title of his 2020 Festschrift, *For Us, but Not to Us*, comes from it

views.name: Historical-grammatical background study
views.who: Craig Keener (*IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament*), John Walton, Victor Matthews and Mark Chavalas (*IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament*); most evangelical scholarship
views.summary: Recover the historical, cultural and linguistic setting of each text so that we hear what the first audience heard, then apply the same message today.
views.strengths: It clears up many puzzles, guards against reading modern ideas into ancient texts, and respects God's choice to speak in history.
views.critiques: Background can become a new expert key that ordinary readers cannot use. Scholars warn of "parallelomania" (Samuel Sandmel's word, 1962) — finding parallels everywhere and over-reading them.

views.name: Social-scientific reading
views.who: Bruce Malina, Jerome Neyrey, David deSilva, Kenneth Bailey
views.summary: Use models from cultural anthropology — honour and shame, patronage, kinship, purity — to understand the social world assumed by the text.
views.strengths: It opens parables, letters and Gospel scenes in vivid ways, and helps readers see grace, faith and family in their relational setting.
views.critiques: Models can be applied too rigidly, as if all ancient people thought alike. Bailey's use of modern Middle Eastern village life has been questioned as a guide to first-century practice.

views.name: Canonical and theological reading
views.who: Brevard Childs, Christopher Seitz, Kevin Vanhoozer, many Catholic and Orthodox readers
views.summary: The most important context of any passage is the whole Bible as the church received it. Reconstructed backgrounds help, but they must not replace the canonical text and the faith of the church.
views.strengths: It keeps attention on the text we actually have and on its witness to God, not on speculative reconstructions.
views.critiques: It can neglect history and leave hard cultural questions unanswered, so readers import their own assumptions without noticing.

views.name: Jesus as the final context
views.who: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Tommy Miller; in other forms Richard Hays and many Church Fathers
views.summary: Culture explains how the first hearers understood God's word; Jesus shows what God was always saying through it (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). The last and deepest context of every text is the life, death and resurrection of Jesus.
views.strengths: It keeps background study from becoming mere history and explains why the New Testament reads the Old so freely in light of Christ.
views.critiques: Critics worry it can skip the hard historical work or treat the Old Testament's culture as only an obstacle. Traditional scholars add that the first meaning must still be heard on its own terms before it is seen in Christ.

views.name: Majority-world and contextual reading
views.who: E. Randolph Richards and Brandon O'Brien (*Misreading Scripture with Western Eyes*); the *Africa Bible Commentary*; the *South Asia Bible Commentary*
views.summary: Readers from cultures built on honour, extended family and patronage often notice what Western individualist readers miss. Every culture both helps and hinders reading.
views.strengths: It shows that the Western reading is not the neutral one, and it honours the insight of the global church, including Indian and Tamil readers.
views.critiques: It can swap one cultural lens for another — reading modern Asian or African customs into the text is still eisegesis. The ancient world must be studied, not assumed.

misreadings.topic: "If it is cultural, it does not apply to us"
misreadings.popular: Some readers fear that once we start explaining passages by their culture, we will explain the Bible away. Others use "that was just their culture" to set aside any command they find difficult.
misreadings.inContext: Context does not remove the message; it locates it. A command given in one culture carries a principle that crosses cultures. Paul himself says the Old Testament was written for our learning (Rom 15:4) and for our admonition (1 Cor 10:11), even though it was first given to Israel.
misreadings.defence: Traditional evangelical scholars agree that context is essential, but warn against using "culture" as an escape. The real disagreements are over which practices are cultural expressions and which are timeless — for example head coverings (1 Cor 11:5-6) or women teaching (1 Tim 2:12). Scholars on both sides use careful criteria rather than preference.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Without a fair method, people either apply ancient customs rigidly or dismiss whatever is uncomfortable. Both bypass what God was actually saying.

misreadings.topic: The Prodigal Son is only about one sinner coming home
misreadings.popular: The parable is usually preached as the story of an individual sinner who wastes his life, repents and comes back to God, who forgives him.
misreadings.inContext: Luke sets the parable in a dispute: religious leaders complained that Jesus welcomed sinners (Luke 15:1-2). The three stories of lost sheep, coin and son build to a story with two lost sons. The older brother, who never left home, stands outside the feast at the end. The father's costly, shame-bearing love reaches out to both.
misreadings.defence: Traditional scholars agree the older brother is central and the setting is Luke 15:1-2. They also rightly say the younger son's return is a true picture of repentance, so preaching it as a conversion story is a fair application, as long as the older brother is not forgotten.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If the older brother disappears, religious people never hear that the story is also about them. The parable calls insiders as well as outsiders to the Father's feast.

discuss: What does "written for us but not to us" mean to you? Does it make the Bible feel closer or further away?
Which part of the Prodigal Son table surprised you most? How does it change the story?
Which customs in your own culture help you understand the Bible's world? Which might mislead you?
Can you think of an idiom in your language that would be misunderstood if translated word for word?
How should we decide whether a command is a cultural expression or a timeless principle?
practice: Choose one New Testament letter and, before reading it, find out who wrote it, to whom, when and why. Then read it in one sitting.
Read John 3:1-15 in two different translations and note every place where they differ.
Look up one cultural topic in the Context section of this app (honour and shame, patronage or covenant) and find two passages it helps you understand.
